news.title: [SMM News] Zambia Aims to Boost EV and Battery Production to Maximize Value from Critical MineralsZambia is seeking investment in battery and electric vehicle manufacturing to retain more value from its mineral resources. The latest investment appeal reinforces that ambition without announcing a plant capacity or commissioning schedule. Neighbouring Zimbabwe offers a regional example of progress in lithium processing, although concentrates still dominate its lithium export earnings. Zambia seeks investment across the battery and EV chain In a statement made on the 22nd of October 2026, the Zambia Development Agency (ZDA) had urged investment in EV, battery and component manufacturing near mineral sources. Speaking at the Zambia Mining Insaka CEO Roundtable, emphasis on predictable policy and which value-added products Zambia should export through the Lobito Corridor. The statement gives no committed investment value, plant capacity or start date. Lithium potential still requires commercial definition ZDA also highlighted lithium alongside nickel and manganese, which are major battery materials. Lithium was already included in Zambia’s National Critical Minerals Strategy 2024-2028. The strategy records occurrences around Mapatizya in Southern Province, Nyimba and Lundazi in Eastern Province, and several districts in Central Province. Occurrences alone do not establish commercially mineable reserves or a reliable supply of battery-grade feedstock. The ambition also builds on the Zambia–DRC battery initiative. UNECA reported in April 2024 that the countries were reviewing a pre-feasibility study for a joint battery and EV special economic zone, following a March 2023 framework agreement. Zimbabwe adds lithium sulphate to its export mix MMCZ figures put Zimbabwe’s lithium export sales at approximately US$2.159 billion in January-September 2026. Lithium sulphate contributed US$190.52 million on an estimated 33,807 mt, compared with no recorded sulphate sales in the corresponding period of 2025. Mining Zimbabwe attributed the sulphate exports to Huayou’s Arcadia operation. Huayou said its Zimbabwe base held its first lithium sulphate shipment ceremony on 25 April 2026. Its ATZ refinery is located beside the Prospect Lithium Zimbabwe (PLZ) concentrator in the Arcadia mining area and has a stated design capacity of 50,000 mt of lithium sulphate a year in product capacity. Zimbabwe lithium export sales in January-September 2026 Product Value US$ million Share of reported total Spodumene concentrate 1,812 83.9% Lithium sulphate 190.52 8.8% Petalite 155.29 7.2% Reported total ≈2,159 100% Zimbabwe’s government has maintained its stated plan to ban lithium concentrate exports from January 2027. A February 2026 suspension was followed by a resumption under export quotas. The pace of new processing capacity and any transition arrangements will be important for 2027 feedstock availability. Lithium sulphate is an intermediate product Lithium sulphate requires further conversion into lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide for battery materials. Component and cell manufacturing, followed by pack and vehicle assembly, involve additional processes and inputs. Spodumene assessments fell about 24 percent from 9 to 30 October The three Zimbabwean spodumene grades fell by 24.0-24.6% between early to late October 2026. All three declined in each of the three weekly comparisons. The 6% Li₂O assessment reached US$1,295/mt on 30 October, within a range of US$1,250-1,340/mt. SMM assessment values supplied in the draft. CIF Chinese main ports, dry basis. Historical values were not independently retrieved from the public pages; see the data note. Zimbabwean spodumene assessments in October 2026 Grade 9 Oct 16 Oct 23 Oct 30 Oct 30 Oct range 9-30 Oct change 6% Li₂O 1,705 1,480 1,405 1,295 1,250-1,340 -410 (-24.0%) 5.5% Li₂O 1,585 1,400 1,315 1,200 1,160-1,240 -385 (-24.3%) 5% Li₂O 1,485 1,320 1,225 1,120 1,030-1,210 -365 (-24.6%) US$/mt, dry basis; CIF Chinese main ports. Fe₂O₃ ≤1.5%, mica ≤3%, moisture ≤15%. Values and ranges are from the supplied draft; changes are recalculated. In the week to 30 October, the 6% grade fell US$110/mt (7.83%), the 5.5% grade fell US$115/mt (8.75%) and the 5% grade fell US$105/mt (8.57%). The largest absolute weekly decline occurred from 9 to 16 October, at US$225/mt, US$185/mt and US$165/mt, respectively. SMM view For Zambia, the next test is whether investment promotion produces projects with defined feedstock, financing, reliable power and customer offtake. Chemical processing, battery cell production and EV assembly need separate capacity targets and commissioning milestones. Zimbabwe’s experience demonstrates a route into intermediate chemicals; however, does not establish the economics of a Zambian battery or EV plant. Progress should be judged by disclosed resource assessments, financed plants, commissioned throughput and executed offtakes, with separate milestones for chemical processing, cell production and EV assembly.Nov 18, 2026 18:50 (GMT+8)

news.title: Lithium Market: From End-User Consumption and Active Destocking to the Mismatch in Marginal Procurement [SMM Analysis]1. Core Conclusions The key issue in the current lithium market is not a collapse in end demand, but rather that active destocking across the supply chain has amplified changes in end-user demand, leaving upstream producers facing marginal procurement demand that is significantly weaker than actual consumption. Over the past month, the inventory structure has changed materially: destocking has been concentrated mainly at the downstream level, while inventories held by lithium salt producers and other market participants have increased. This structure suggests that the current inventory drawdown should not simply be interpreted as evidence of strong spot procurement. On the contrary, downstream cathode material producers are meeting production needs by reducing raw material inventories, while remaining cautious on incremental spot purchases. Inventories are gradually shifting from consumption inventories toward producer-held and trading inventories. At the same time, cathode producers do not rely entirely on self-procured lithium salts. Some operate under customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements, whereby battery manufacturers, affiliated companies, or designated upstream suppliers provide lithium salts directly to cathode producers for processing. As a result, cathode output and cathode producers’ own lithium salt procurement are not necessarily correlated on a one-to-one basis. When the share of customer-supplied lithium salts rises, cathode production can remain elevated even without a corresponding increase in market-based spot procurement. The market can therefore experience tight supply-demand balances, declining inventories, and weak prices at the same time. The reason is that prices are primarily driven by marginal procurement rather than by end consumption itself. As long as the supply chain remains in an active destocking phase, and part of cathode production continues to be supported by long-term contracts and customer-supplied lithium salts, cathode and battery producers can maintain relatively high production levels while significantly reducing their purchases in the open market. A genuine price inflection point is more likely to emerge when the supply chain shifts from “destocking” to “stable inventories” or even “restocking.” At that point, normal production demand and inventory replenishment demand could be released simultaneously, creating procurement growth that is significantly stronger than the growth in end demand. 2. Total Inventories Are Still Falling, but Inventory Ownership Has Changed From an aggregate perspective, lithium carbonate inventories are still trending lower. However, the structure of this drawdown is notably different from a conventional demand-driven destocking cycle. The most significant feature is that downstream inventories have fallen sharply on a weekly basis, while inventories held by lithium salt producers and other market participants have increased. This indicates that inventory ownership is shifting away from downstream consumers toward lithium salt producers and trading intermediaries. Downstream cathode producers are increasingly operating with lean inventories rather than actively rebuilding raw material stocks during a falling-price environment. Lithium salt producers, meanwhile, have shown some reluctance to sell aggressively at low prices, while trading intermediaries are increasingly performing functions related to price positioning, title transfer, and tactical inventory management. A more accurate description of the current inventory trend is therefore that total inventories are still declining, but inventories are migrating from downstream consumers toward upstream suppliers and intermediate trading channels. This change is important for assessing price elasticity. Downstream inventories primarily serve as production buffer stocks and are relatively rigid, whereas inventories held by traders and lithium salt producers are more price-sensitive. If prices rebound, these latter inventories are more likely to return to the market as potential spot supply, thereby creating upside resistance. 3. Cathode Material Output Has Not Fallen in Parallel, Indicating a Decoupling Between “Consumption” and “Procurement” Cathode material production remains relatively high. According to SMM data, weekly LFP output is approximately 141,600 mt, while ternary cathode material output is around 18,000 mt. Ternary output has declined for nine consecutive weeks, but LFP production remains elevated. Assuming approximately 0.24 mt of lithium carbonate consumption per tonne of LFP, weekly theoretical lithium carbonate consumption associated with LFP production alone would be around 34,000 mt LCE, exceeding the total lithium carbonate inventory reported at cathode producers. This should not, however, be interpreted simply as meaning that downstream inventories are insufficient to support one week of production. First, visible SMM inventory does not capture all lithium salt resources available to cathode producers, which may also include in-transit material, long-term contract deliveries, and raw materials already in the production process. More importantly, customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements are relatively common in the cathode industry. Under such arrangements, part of the lithium salts consumed by cathode producers is not purchased directly by the cathode producer itself, but instead supplied by battery manufacturers, affiliated entities, or designated suppliers. Cathode producers’ visible inventories and self-procured volumes therefore cannot be treated as equivalent to their total lithium salt availability or actual consumption. A more reasonable interpretation is that visible downstream lithium carbonate inventories have been compressed to relatively low levels, but cathode producers can still maintain production through long-term contracts, customer-supplied lithium salts, and continuous deliveries. This is one of the most important current market features: cathode output has not declined materially, but cathode producers’ own procurement and willingness to purchase in the spot market have clearly weakened. After the pre-holiday restocking cycle ended in October, some cathode producers continued to reduce raw material inventories. Procurement appetite among ternary producers has been particularly weak due to continued production cuts, while LFP producers, despite maintaining high output, have also tended to purchase only on a just-in-time basis, relying more heavily on long-term contracts, customer-supplied lithium salts, and lean inventory management. The market therefore needs to distinguish clearly between “actual lithium salt consumption” and “cathode producers’ own procurement.” Especially when customer-supplied material accounts for a high share of input supply, elevated cathode production does not necessarily translate into stronger open-market buying. 4. Why Can Upstream Orders Weaken Sharply Even if End Demand Does Not? The key relationship is that procurement depends on actual consumption, inventory changes, and the share of customer-supplied material. For a producer relying entirely on self-procurement, procurement can be approximated as: Procurement = Actual Consumption + Change in Inventory For cathode producers that also receive customer-supplied lithium salts, the volume supplied by customers or affiliated parties must be deducted from their own market procurement. Therefore, when cathode producers actively destock while the share of customer-supplied material rises, their market-based procurement can fall well below actual production consumption. For example, assume a cathode producer consumes 100 units of lithium salts per week. If inventories are stable and all material is self-procured, procurement would be approximately 100 units. If the producer actively reduces inventories by 20 units, procurement may fall to 80 units. If a further 20 units are supplied by a customer, the cathode producer’s own open-market procurement may decline to just 60 units. This illustrates that upstream suppliers can experience a sharp contraction in visible buying even if actual production demand is unchanged. This explains why the market can simultaneously observe stable end demand and weak lithium salt buying. The underlying reason is that inventory cycles and supply arrangements jointly amplify changes in end demand. news.title: Panama Plans Cobre Panamá Public Dialogue for January 2027; Company Accepts Five PreconditionsPanama’s interministerial commission announced on November 26 that Australian consultancy Spektrum will lead the public participation process concerning Cobre Panamá’s future, with formal community dialogue scheduled to begin in January 2027. Conducted under the Escazú Agreement, the process will collect feedback through online and in-person channels to inform the government’s decision. First Quantum subsidiary Minera Panamá accepted the government’s five preconditions on November 23: 1. State ownership of mineral resources: All underground mineral resources belong to Panama. 2. Maximum benefits for Panama: Any agreement must maximise economic and social benefits, including employment and development opportunities for Panamanians. 3. National sovereignty: Panama retains exclusive authority over its territory, waters and airspace. 4. Environmental protection: Operations must meet the highest applicable environmental standards, with effective independent oversight, verification and public disclosure. 5. Legal compliance: Any agreement or subsequent decision must fully comply with Panama’s Constitution and existing laws. The government also requires any agreement to include a company-funded, verifiable and definitive mine closure plan with no extensions, alongside the resolution of arbitration proceedings against Panama. Acceptance of these conditions does not constitute approval to restart the mine; a final decision remains subject to public participation and subsequent procedures.12 hours ago
